taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes deep mtDNA structure within U. ornatus and that its phylogeography deserves further study (Crother 2017); ADW lists it as 'Tree Lizard'.
fieldMarks: Small, slim lizard (about 3.8-5.9 cm) with a body and tail patterned with blotches or irregular crossbars in black, dark brown, tan or gray to match the local substrate.
Two bands of enlarged scales run down the back with a series of smaller scales between them; base of the tail is usually rusty.
Adult males have blue to blue-green belly patches with a metallic sheen and a green, blue-green, orange or yellow throat patch (dewlap).
Females have a white belly, with a white, orange or yellow throat.
behavior: Perches on trees, rocks and fence posts and ambushes spiders, beetles, ants, termites and other insects from an elevated, motionless position.
Hunts from dawn into the late afternoon; males hold small overlapping territories with a dominance hierarchy in which the heaviest male dominates.
Aggregates in winter hibernacula from mid-November to late February; climbs high into trees for protection.
habitat: Riparian forest (mesquite, oaks, cottonwoods), rocky terrain, and the sides of buildings and fence posts near streams and rivers; also desert with or without trees, sheltering in shrubs, up to about 2,770 m.
range: Southwestern United States and northern Mexico: southeastern California, southern Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico and southwest/central Texas, south to Sonora, Sinaloa, Chihuahua and Coahuila. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Long-tailed brush lizard (Urosaurus graciosus)
lookalikes.howToTell: Tail more than twice the body length and no row of smaller scales down the middle of the enlarged dorsal band.
